title: Gathered ribbon stitch
subtitle: A running stitch along one ribbon edge gathered into a ruched blossom and applied to the fabric
excerpt: Gathered ribbon stitch works a running stitch along one long edge of a short length of silk ribbon, then draws the thread to gather the ribbon into a ruffled blossom shape. The gathered ribbon is then secured to the fabric with small stitches, giving a three-dimensional ruched flower.
sourceNotes: Gathered and ruched ribbon techniques documented in 19th-century needlework and dressmaking manuals. Silk ribbon embroidery application as standard in 20th-century ribbon embroidery references.

content.text: Gathered ribbon stitch builds a three-dimensional flower by gathering the ribbon before it is fixed to the fabric. A running stitch travels along one edge of a short length of silk ribbon; pulling the thread draws the ribbon into a ruffled ring or crescent. The gathered piece is then laid on the fabric and held down with tiny stitches at the centre and around the edge, where the natural folds of the gathering create the appearance of petals or a full blown blossom.

items.label: Ribbon
items.value: 7 mm or 13 mm pure silk ribbon; cut a length 3 to 4 times the finished diameter of the flower

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Firm cotton, silk, or linen mounted in a hoop

items.label: Needle
items.value: Chenille needle size 16 or 18 for threading ribbon; fine embroidery needle size 9 for the gathering running stitch and the attaching stitches

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 15 cm embroidery hoop; working in the hoop keeps the ground fabric stable while you apply the gathered blossom

content.text: Cut the ribbon to the required length. Thread a fine embroidery needle with a strong single strand of thread in a colour that matches the ribbon. Knot the end.

Work a running stitch along one long edge of the ribbon, taking even stitches of about 3 mm. Keep the stitches close to the edge but not so close that the thread tears through the ribbon when gathered.

Pull the gathering thread gently until the ribbon forms a round blossom shape. Adjust the gathers so they are evenly distributed. Do not pull so tight that the ribbon folds collapse against each other; you want visible folds that read as petals.
If the ribbon forms a circle, fold one end under the other to close the join neatly. For an open crescent or bud shape, leave the ends as they are or fold them under at an angle.

Hold the gathered blossom against the fabric. Thread the fine needle with a matching thread and use small stitches to attach the flower at its centre and at a few points around its edge. The stitches at the centre can be covered with a French knot or bead. The stitches at the edge should be hidden within the ribbon folds.

items.symptom: The flower looks stiff and the folds are squashed flat
items.cause: The gathering thread was pulled too tight, or too many attaching stitches were added.
items.fix: Gather only until the blossom is lightly ruffled. Use the minimum number of attaching stitches needed to hold it down: one at the centre and three or four at the edges. Avoid stitching through the top of the folds.

items.symptom: The gathering thread pulls through the ribbon edge
items.cause: The running stitch was placed too close to the raw edge, or the thread is too fine for the tension applied.
items.fix: Work the running stitch at least 3 mm from the edge. Use a slightly thicker thread for gathering, or work two parallel rows of running stitch 1 mm apart and gather both together.

items.symptom: The blossom lifts away from the fabric at the edges
items.cause: Not enough attaching stitches were added around the perimeter.
items.fix: Add a few more small stitches inside the outer fold of the blossom, catching the ribbon down. Tuck the stitch under a fold so it is hidden.

content.text: Gathered ribbon flowers pair well with
leaves and buds in compositions that need one large focal blossom surrounded by smaller stitch-built elements. They are effective for roses, peonies, and full chrysanthemums.
